lines: The night of April 22nd, 1951.
Over the shallow fords of the Imjin River, a strange sound begins to spread.
Gongs. Whistles. And bugles.
s01.label: Dramatization

lines: Behind that sound, the footsteps of tens of thousands of men start to cut through the water.
On the hills south of the river stood a British battalion of barely seven hundred men.
Coming at them: forty thousand.
On paper, this was never supposed to be a fight at all.
And yet these seven hundred men held out for three days.
And those three days would change the fate of Seoul.
So what kept these seven hundred men standing?
No water, almost no ammunition, and every road back cut off behind them.
s05.label: Dramatization

question.text:
Cut off and outnumbered more than ten to one,
how did one British battalion
hold off an entire Chinese army for three days?

lines: The answer lies in a tradition one regiment had guarded for a hundred and fifty years,
and in the quiet decision of one battalion commander.
s06.label: Dramatization

lines: The Battle of the Imjin River, and the Gloster Battalion at Solma-ri.
Today, we follow those three days and nights, one move at a time, across the map.
s07.title: Battle of the Imjin River
s07.sub: The Last Stand of the Glosters at Solma-ri · 1951

lines: Before we begin,
if you want stories like this one to keep being told, please subscribe and hit the like button.
s08.title: Help Us Keep These Battles Remembered

lines: Let's turn the clock back a little.
That spring, the Chinese army was preparing a massive offensive meant to flip the entire war.
s09.label: Chinese soldiers (Mar. 1951)
chapter: The Spring Offensive Aimed at Seoul

lines: It would become known as the Chinese Spring Offensive of April 1951.
More than three hundred thousand troops were committed.
And the objective was one city. Seoul.
There was even word that they meant to retake Seoul in time for May Day, the first of May.
Only three months earlier, Seoul had already fallen to the enemy once more, before being won back.
The man directing this offensive was the Chinese commander in Korea, Peng Dehuai.
He massed his main strength on the western front, choosing to cross the Imjin and drive straight down on Seoul.
That road ran through Kaesong, Munsan, and Choksong.
s12.name: Peng Dehuai

lines: South of the Imjin, the UN forces held a defensive line called Line Kansas.
But the troops on that line were spread thin,
and no one knew exactly when, or where, the blow would land.
If Seoul fell for a third time, the course of the war, and any hope of a ceasefire, could change completely.
And squarely across that invasion route lay the Imjin River.
The unit holding more than nineteen kilometers of that riverbank was the British 29th Infantry Brigade.
It was an absurdly wide front for a single brigade.
Normally, a distance like that would call for two or three times as many men.
The brigade had three British battalions, the Glosters, the Northumberland Fusiliers and the Royal Ulster Rifles, plus a Belgian battalion,
backed by artillery and Centurion tanks.
The problem was the space in between.
Between one battalion and the next, there were gaps several kilometers wide.
At the far left end of that line, guarding the road down to Seoul, stood one unit.
The 1st Battalion, the Gloucestershire Regiment. The Glosters.
So what happens if this battalion breaks?
The enemy pours straight down toward Uijeongbu and Seoul.
And the flank of every other British battalion to their right is laid wide open.
One battalion, in effect, was holding the door handle of the entire front.
s20.label: Dramatization

lines: The Glosters carry one very unusual tradition.
Their soldiers wear the regimental badge not only on the front of their caps, but on the back as well.
s21.label: Dramatization

lines: It honors a battle in Egypt a hundred and fifty years earlier, when the regiment was attacked from front and rear at once, and fought back to back, and won.
Enemy in front. Enemy behind.
No one could have imagined that badge would become reality again on the Imjin.
quotes: The Regiment That Fought Back to Back

lines: Keep that badge in mind for a moment.
Because in this battle, it stops being just a decoration.
The battalion commander was Lieutenant Colonel James Carne.
A man of few words, he was known for the pipe he always seemed to have clenched in his teeth.
s24.name: James Carne

lines: The battalion had arrived in Korea the previous autumn, and had already been through a brutal winter of fighting.
Under his command were roughly seven hundred and fifty men.
s25.label: Glosters advancing with Centurion tanks (Mar. 1951)

lines: They had set foot in Korea as the winter of 1950 was closing in.
In temperatures that swung around twenty below zero, they had already fallen back once to south of Seoul, and then fought their way north again.
s25b.label: Dramatization

lines: The battalion dug in company by company across the hills around Choksong in Paju, on the slopes of Mount Kamak.
A Company took the hill jutting out toward the river, known as Castle Hill.
And behind battalion headquarters rose one small peak.
Two hundred and thirty-five meters high.
It would later be known as Gloster Hill.
Cut a cross-section through the Imjin valley that April, and you can see why this ground was so dangerous.
The river is low, and the hills are not very high.
s28.title: Imjin River → Hill 235 · North–South Profile

lines: But this layout had a fatal weakness.
The companies were simply too far apart.
In places, they were too far apart to cover one another with fire.
With so few men, there was no other choice.
Colonel Carne knew about the gaps, but he had no one left to fill them.
s30.label: Dramatization

lines: Beyond the battalion's left flank stood the South Korean 1st Division.
But between those two units, too, lay a wide gap of hills and valleys.
Each held its own ground, without ever quite joining hands.
And then there was the river running in front of the battalion.
In April, the Imjin runs shallow.
At the fords, the water came up no higher than a man's waist.
The river was no obstacle at all. It was simply a road you could walk across.
The soldiers called that spot Gloster Crossing.
s33.label: Dramatization

lines: Among the men were hardened veterans of the Second World War,
but many were young conscripts of about twenty, freshly shipped across the sea.
These rocky, unfamiliar mountains were nothing like the green fields of home in Gloucestershire.
s34.label: British troops on the march in Korea

lines: That April, azaleas were blooming on the slopes of Mount Kamak.
By day the men dug trenches, and by night they sent patrols across toward the far bank.
For days, the patrols found not so much as a shadow of the enemy.
s35.label: Dramatization

lines: For days, the front was strangely quiet.
The darkness across the river already knew that this calm was the silence before the storm.
s36.label: Dramatization

lines: The night of April 22nd. Moonlight was shining on the river.
Near the ford lay a platoon-sized ambush patrol led by Lieutenant Guy Temple.
As midnight drew near, dark shapes appeared on the water.
Temple's patrol is said to have stopped the enemy crossing in midstream several times that night.
But this was not an enemy one platoon could hold back.
s39.label: Dramatization

lines: It wasn't one or two men.
They came in lines, wading across without end.
s40.label: Dramatization

lines: The patrol opened fire all at once.
The leading ranks fell into the river.
And then something strange.
The next rank walked straight over the spot where the first had fallen.
They fell, and still more came.
s42.label: Dramatization

lines: Temple's platoon only pulled back after firing until its ammunition ran out.
The enemy who crossed the river that night was the Chinese 63rd Army.
Three divisions. Tens of thousands of men.
The 63rd Army's orders were clear.
Cross the Imjin, smash through the British positions in one blow, and throw open the road to Uijeongbu.
By their calculations, the whole job would take a single night.
s44.head: Imjin Breakthrough · Mission Summary

lines: And that is when the sound begins.
Gongs and cymbals, shrill whistles, and long, wailing bugles.
s45.label: Dramatization

lines: The Chinese used these sounds to signal the direction of attack, and at the same time to grind down the nerves of the enemy.
Noise echoing from every side, below a pitch-black ridge.
The terror of not knowing where they were coming from, or how many.
And the attack that night was not aimed at the Glosters alone.
The Belgian battalion, posted north of the river, was cut off, and the Fusiliers on the right were hit all night long.
The whole brigade was engulfed in flames at the same time.
The British artillery poured shells out all night without a pause.
It's said the gun barrels glowed red-hot.
s48.label: UN artillery firing in defense of a position (1951)

lines: Still the waves did not shrink.
Cut down one battalion, and another battalion stood right behind it.
This was the Chinese human-wave attack.
The first Chinese blade struck the most exposed position, A Company on Castle Hill.
Grenades fell like rain, and bayonets clashed between the trenches.
Through that long night, the positions on the hill changed hands again and again.
By daybreak, A Company had lost nearly half its men.
s51.label: Dramatization

lines: And this was only the beginning.
The real ordeal would come after sunrise.
The morning of April 23rd.
A Company's commander, Major Pat Angier, is killed on the hill.
With its commander gone, the company was on the verge of collapse.
s53.label: Dramatization

lines: By a cruel coincidence, it was Saint George's Day, the feast of England's patron saint.
At home, it was a day for wearing a rose on your chest,
but up on that hill, no one had a moment to mark it.
s54.sub: England's National Day · Saint George's Day

lines: Then a young officer pulls himself to his feet.
Lieutenant Philip Curtis.
s55.label: Grave of Lt. Curtis, UN Memorial Cemetery, Busan · aged 24

lines: At the top of Castle Hill, the Chinese had seized a machine-gun post.
That one position was pinning down the entire company.
Curtis had already been shot.
His men tried to hold him back, but he shook them off and charged up the slope alone, grenades in hand.
s57.label: Dramatization

lines: Hit again, he went down, then got up and crawled on.
And at the moment he threw his last grenade into the post, he died on the spot.
He would be awarded Britain's highest decoration for valor, the Victoria Cross.
It was the final charge of a twenty-four-year-old officer.
And his sacrifice bought A Company the time it needed to get off the hill.
When daylight came, the Chinese attacks paused for breath.
British guns and UN fighter-bombers owned the daytime sky.
But even then, the enemy never stopped moving through the hills and valleys.
s60.label: UN fighter-bomber dropping napalm (1952)

lines: But the real danger was not in front of the hill. It was behind it.
The Chinese weren't only hammering the front.
Thousands of them had slipped through those wide gaps between the battalions,
and come all the way down into the Solma-ri valley, behind the Glosters.
The supply route was cut. The way out was blocked.
Enemy in front. Enemy behind.
The legend of the badge on the back of their caps had come to life.
The only link left between brigade headquarters and the battalion was a thin thread of radio.
And over that radio, the battalion's situation grew worse by the hour.
s64.label: Dramatization

lines: That night, the remaining companies were attacked one after another.
On the ridges held by D and B Companies, grenades and machine guns never fell silent all night.
And with every dawn, the empty places in the trenches grew more obvious.
s65.label: Dramatization

lines: Colonel Carne made his decision.
He would pull in all his scattered companies and gather them in one place.
That place was Hill 235.
Just getting the companies up to the hill was a battle in itself.
They carried their wounded on stretchers and crawled up the ridges, loaded with heavy mortars and machine guns.
s67.label: Dramatization

lines: Men who fell behind in the darkness never came back.
And the battalion that gathered there now had nowhere left to retreat, not a single step.
s68.label: Dramatization

lines: The Glosters had become an island, surrounded by the enemy on all sides, a full three hundred and sixty degrees.
April 24th.
The men gathered on the hill numbered barely four hundred.
After two straight nights of fighting, their canteens were empty.
The ammunition boxes were starting to show their bottoms.
Even the radio batteries were running down.
Once that last link to brigade went dead, the battalion would be truly cut off from the world.
s72.label: Dramatization

lines: The wounded lay on the floors of the trenches, waiting for a single mouthful of water.
And the path down to the valley to fetch that water was already inside the enemy's field of fire.
s73.label: Dramatization

lines: The men counted out what ammunition was left and shared it, round by round.
So many rounds per rifle, so many belts per machine gun.
Not one shot could be wasted.
s74.label: Dramatization

lines: They had to wait until the enemy was right on top of them, and pull the trigger only when they could not miss.
Hunger and thirst, and a third night without sleep.
Their eyes were already hollow and sunken.
And yet not one of them left his trench.
s76.label: UN soldiers catching their breath on a hilltop (Korea)

lines: Some companies never made it up to the hill.
B Company, holding a separate ridge, beat off several attacks through the night, but in the end its ammunition ran out and its position was overrun.
It is said that only a handful of its men made it up to Hill 235 alive.
With the battalion was a troop of British mortars as well.
They too kept firing to the very end, and shared the Glosters' fate.
s78.label: Dramatization

lines: From the rear, there was an attempt to save them.
A Filipino battalion pushed into the Solma-ri valley together with British tanks.
The Filipinos had come from a distant island nation far to the south.
They too threw themselves into that gorge to rescue British soldiers in a foreign land.
s80.label: Dramatization

lines: But the narrow gorge road was a Chinese killing ground.
When the lead tank was knocked out and blocked the road,
the relief force never reached the hill, and had to turn back.
There is a painful story told about this moment.
Brigadier Tom Brodie, in classic British understatement, is said to have told his American superior that things were, quote, a bit sticky.
quotes: Understated report · A crisis that never got through

lines: That restrained phrase, the story goes, never conveyed how serious the crisis really was.
Meanwhile, up on the hill, an entire battalion was on the edge of disappearing.
s83.label: Dramatization

lines: Still, Colonel Carne did not waver.
He is said to have strolled calmly between the trenches as shells fell, patting his men on the shoulder.
As long as their commander was on his feet, his men could not fall either.
s84.label: Dramatization

lines: That night, the Chinese came again.
Mortar rounds plowed up the ridgeline,
and the men fought with bayonets, rifle butts, and even rocks.
s86.label: Dramatization

lines: Then, at dawn on April 25th,
the battalion adjutant, Captain Anthony Farrar-Hockley, called for Drum Major Philip Buss and gave him an order.
Sound the bugle. Every call you know, except the retreat.
s87.label: Dramatization

lines: Over the smoke-covered hill, a British bugle rang out.
A bugle, answering the gongs.
A cheer burst out among the men.
It was their answer: we are still here.
s89.label: Dramatization

lines: The morning of April 25th.
Over the radio, the final message came through.
s90.label: Dramatization

lines: There would be no more relief.
Artillery support would soon end.
Find your own way out.
s91.head: Final Instructions to the Glosters · Summary

lines: In effect, it was the last order the battalion would ever receive.
That morning, UN fighter-bombers swept in around the hill with machine guns and napalm.
It was cover, meant to open even the smallest gap for one last escape.
Colonel Carne called his company commanders together.
And he told them, calmly,
from here on, each of you use your own judgment, break through, and make for our lines.
s94.label: Dramatization

lines: If the battalion moved as one body, it could be wiped out all at once.
Only by splitting up could anyone hope to make it home.
Men who had held out together for three days now had to stake their lives on different paths.
But not everyone could leave.
There were men too badly wounded to move.
s96.label: Evacuating the wounded (1951)

lines: The medical officer, Captain Bob Hickey, and the chaplain, the Reverend Sam Davies, chose to stay on the hill.
They would remain beside the wounded.
s97.label: Dramatization

lines: Even though it meant certain capture.
A doctor and a priest gave up their own chance to escape.
And to guard the backs of the comrades who were leaving,
some men stayed on the ridge, gripping their machine guns, to the very end.
s99.label: Dramatization

lines: Shortly after ten in the morning, the men began going down the hill in small groups.
As they half ran, half slid down the steep slopes, Chinese machine guns opened up behind them.
s100.label: Dramatization

lines: The breakout was desperate.
Most of the men headed south, and were captured by the Chinese.
Colonel Carne, too, was taken prisoner.
So was the adjutant, Captain Farrar-Hockley.
In the prison camps, he tried to escape again and again,
and he later rose to become a British Army general, and wrote the record of this battle.
s102.sub: Adjutant, 1st Glosters · Later a British Army General

lines: Only one group, led by D Company's commander, Major Mike Harvey, chose a different path.
Instead of going south, where the enemy expected, they first turned north, swinging in a wide arc over the mountains.
Even that final stretch was not easy.
When the exhausted men came down into a valley, friendly tanks mistook them for the enemy and opened fire.
s104.label: Dramatization

lines: Some fell on the very threshold of safety.
Only after a friendly spotter plane circling overhead recognized them and signaled the tanks,
were they able to come home alive.
s105.label: Dramatization

lines: Of that group, only about forty men finally reached friendly lines.
A battalion that began with seven hundred and fifty men.
Those who broke through and made it back numbered only a few dozen.
More than five hundred men were taken prisoner,
and many of them would spend more than two years in prison camps, until the war was over.
s108.label: British prisoners captured by Chinese forces
chapter: The Three Days That Saved Seoul

lines: The prisoners were marched hundreds of kilometers north, to camps near the Yalu River.
Through hunger and cold, more than a few never came home.
s108b.label: Dramatization

lines: So were these three days a defeat?
Judged by the numbers alone, it might look that way.
But in those three days, the Chinese 63rd Army's timetable fell completely apart.
The fastest road to Seoul had been blocked by one small hill.
The whole British 29th Brigade had faced tens of thousands of men,
and some estimates put Chinese losses as high as ten thousand.
And the Glosters were not the only ones who bled.
That same day, the Fusiliers and the Ulsters also had to fight their way back down narrow valleys.
Over those three days, the brigade's killed, wounded and missing came to more than a thousand.
But the weight of those three days cannot be measured in numbers alone.
Had this line broken on the very first night, the Chinese might have reached the gates of Uijeongbu within a day or two.

question.text:
Cut off and outnumbered more than ten to one,
how did one British battalion
hold off an entire Chinese army for three days?

lines: In the time they bought, UN forces were able to build a solid new defensive line north of Seoul.
And the Chinese Spring Offensive finally ground to a halt at Seoul's doorstep.
callouts: LATE APR. 1951 · NEW LINE NORTH OF SEOUL (APPROX.)

lines: In captivity, Colonel Carne is said to have carved a small cross out of stone.
That cross rests today in Gloucester Cathedral, in England.
s115.label: Dramatization

lines: He reportedly spent much of his captivity in solitary confinement.
Only after the armistice in 1953 was he finally able to go home.
He was awarded the Victoria Cross,
and the whole battalion received the U.S. Presidential Unit Citation.
To this day, the regiment's successors wear that citation on their sleeves.
quotes: Whole Battalion · U.S. Presidential Unit Citation

lines: In Solma-ri, Paju, a British battle memorial still stands in that valley today.
Every April, white-haired veterans and their families gathered before it and bowed their heads.
s118.label: British battle memorial, Solma-ri, Paju

lines: Decades after the war, the old soldiers still came back to this valley, leaning on their canes.
For them, this was the ground where they had buried their friends and left them behind.
s119.label: Dramatization

lines: Paju, too, has held a memorial ceremony here year after year.
Korean soldiers and citizens have laid flowers in the same place, side by side with the British veterans.
s120.label: 75th Anniversary Memorial, Battle of the Imjin (Apr. 2026 · Solma-ri)

lines: Today, nearly all the survivors of those days are gone.
But their names are still carved into the stone.
s121.label: Dramatization

lines: Seven hundred men who fought back to back on the bank of a strange river in a faraway country, for people whose names they never knew.
What they saved was not just one hill. It was a nation's capital.
quotes: Not Just One Hill, But a Nation's Capital

lines: And in that capital, millions of people live their lives today.
If you ever find yourself near Mount Kamak in Paju, take a moment to remember the valley of Solma-ri.
s123.label: Dramatization

lines: That's all for today's battle.
If this story meant something to you, please subscribe, like, and share it with someone who should hear it.
We'll see you on the next battlefield.
s124.title:
April 1951 · Solma-ri, Paju
The 700 who held for three days.
